dek.text: Dallas runs computer vision cameras on {{number:c5}} brush trucks. Its October briefing says staff review every observation, and it publishes no accuracy figure.

introduction.text: [Dallas mounts computer vision cameras on {{number:c5}} Sanitation brush collection vehicles that already travel its neighborhoods on routine service](c5). [The software is City Detect, which flags possible exterior property and right-of-way conditions for trained staff to review](c3). [The city says no separate Code Compliance patrol routes are created](c6).

[A briefing dated {{date:c2}}](c2) [went to the council's Quality of Life, Arts, and Culture Committee](c1). [It says a computer vision observation is not a confirmed Code violation and that city staff make that call](c4). [It lists calibrating detection accuracy among its next steps](c29). The briefing publishes no accuracy figure.

sections.heading: What the camera does, and what staff do

paragraphs.text: [The briefing says the technology identifies potential exterior conditions](c7) [and helps staff decide which areas to review first](c8). [It says the technology doesn't decide on its own that a violation exists](c9), [doesn't replace a Code Officer's judgment](c10) [and doesn't open formal enforcement from an observation alone](c11). [Staff review every computer generated observation before Code Compliance takes any action](c13).

[In a prioritized inspection a trained Code Officer first reviews the observation and decides whether it calls for a field inspection](c18). [A Code Inspector then goes on site to find out whether a violation exists](c19). [Faces and license plates are blurred inside the system, according to the city's privacy slide](c12).

[The briefing's results table reports {{number:c22}} observations reviewed](c22), [{{number:c23:1}} courtesy notices](c23), [{{number:c24:1}} field inspections](c24), [{{number:c25:1}} voluntary corrections](c25), [{{number:c26:1}} direct abatements](c26) [and {{number:c27:1}} under formal enforcement](c27). The table doesn't say how one row relates to another, so none of these counts can be read as a rate.

[Under the previous approach the first letter a resident received was a formal notice of violation, the first step toward a citation](c15). [Now, when a courtesy notice is used, the first letter is an educational reminder outside the citation process that sets no deadline](c16). [The city says a courtesy notice alone never opens a formal enforcement case](c17).

[An earlier briefing to the Finance Committee is dated {{date:c33}}](c33). [It proposed putting {{number:c34}} AI-enabled cameras on Sanitation brush trucks](c34). [It put the cost at {{money:c36}} a year, covering the cameras with installation, data services, maintenance and replacement support](c36), [and said the city may end the contract at any time on {{number:c37}} days written notice without penalty](c37). [It said there is a human in the loop for all actions](c38).

[A city memo dated {{date:c41}}](c41) [says the cameras go on {{number:c44}} brush and bulky waste trucks, two per vehicle](c44). [It says the technology will issue no automatic citations and that Code Compliance staff will verify every potential violation before acting](c45).

[The city says success is measured by better neighborhood conditions and service delivery rather than by the number of citations generated](c28). [Its next steps include continuing to calibrate detection accuracy and staff validation](c29) [and setting performance measures for accuracy, response, voluntary compliance, resource use and neighborhood outcomes](c30). Those measures are named in the {{date:c2}} briefing as work still to come, and none of them is published in it. How often an observation proved to be a real condition is not stated there.
[The deck closes on its own summary, that technology identifies potential conditions and people make the decisions](c32).
